title: Effects of road traffic noise on sleep: Studies on children and adults
research_question: To evaluate exposure-effect relationships between road traffic noise and sleep quality for children and parents, and to compare sleep assessed by sleep logs and wrist-actigraphy for children and parents.

participants.description: 160 children (9-12 years old) and 160 parents (usually mothers) from residential areas in Sweden exposed to different levels of road traffic noise. Half of the families (79 children, 79 parents) participated in an in-depth study. Participants in the in-depth study had no hearing problems and parents did not work night-shifts.
participants.recruitment: 160 families were selected for the main study based on noise exposure categories and building characteristics. Information on bedroom window position was obtained during interviews.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Road traffic noise levels in residential areas in Sweden. Noise exposure was assessed by calculations (Nordic prediction method) for each participant's apartment (outdoor levels, free field values at the most exposed side). Four LAeq,24h exposure categories: <55, 55-59, 60-64, and >64 dB. Lnight levels outside bedroom windows were also used for parents.

measures.instrument: Self-report questionnaire (0-10 point scale: 'very badly'=0, 'very well'=10) and sleep log (11-point numerical scale: 'very badly'=0, 'very well'=10)
Self-report questionnaire ('Have you felt tired or sleepy in school or in your free time during the past month?' with frequency categories)

measures.construct: Perceived interference with road traffic noise
measures.instrument: Self-report questionnaire ('When you are at home, do you think that noise from road traffic disturbs you or interferes with going to bed to sleep?' with frequency categories for children; 'How often do you feel that road traffic noise cause you difficulties falling asleep?' for parents)
Self-report questionnaire ('Have you had difficulties in falling asleep in the evening during the past month?' with frequency categories) and sleep log
Self-report questionnaire ('Have you woken up during the night in the past month?' with frequency categories) and sleep log (number of awakenings)

measures.construct: Habit of keeping bedroom windows open
measures.instrument: Self-report questionnaire ('Do you usually sleep with windows open if it is not too cold?' with frequency categories) and sleep log
Self-report questionnaire (0-10 point scale: 'tired and without energy'=0, 'alert and well rested'=10) and sleep log (11-point numerical scale: 'tired and sleepy'=0, 'alert and rested'=10)
Sleep log and wrist-actigraphy (Cole-Kripke sleep scoring algorithm)
Sleep log (11-point numerical scale: 'hardly at all'=0, 'twisted and turned all night'=10) and wrist-actigraphy (activity mean, activity index)
Sleep log (button press for lights out/wake up)
Wrist-actigraphy (number of blocks of contiguous wake periods)

mechanisms: Physiological and perceived arousal from noise
Changes in EEG parameters, awakening, motility, subjective sleep quality, heart rate, and mood next day (from previous studies)
Differences in body motility due to age (explaining actigraphy differences between children and parents)
Homeostatic determinants and circadian timing affecting sleepiness, moderated by environmental factors
moderators: Position of bedroom windows (facing most exposed side vs courtyard)
implementation_implications: WHO guidelines recommend sound levels of LAmax 45 dB and LAeq 30 dB inside bedrooms during night time, and LAmax 60 dB and LAeq 40 dB outside bedrooms.

The finding on greater problems with daytime sleepiness in home environments with noise levels above LAeq,24h 55 dB stresses the need for research on the importance of opportunities for restoration in children's home environment.

limitations: Optimal assessment of noise exposure (individual indoor measurements with open/closed windows) was not feasible for all participants.
Night-time noise exposure levels in the highest noise category (>64 dB) might have been overestimated due to uncertainties in traffic load distribution and unknown noise-insulation measures.
Lack of knowledge/control over individual noise exposure, room temperature, and person-related factors in a cross-sectional field study.
Comparisons between studies using different types of actigraphs and different age groups should be made with caution.
Poor correlation between sleep logs and actigraphy for number and duration of awakenings.
Self-reported sleep quality is subjective, while actigraphy may not distinguish between quiet wakefulness and restless sleep.
